claim: Sensory errors induce rapid compensation within a movement.
source: Sensory errors induce two types of behavioral changes: rapid compensation within a movement and longer-term adaptation of subsequent movements.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, representing a foundational concept in sensorimotor control.

claim: Sensory errors induce longer-term adaptation of subsequent movements.
source: Sensory errors induce two types of behavioral changes: rapid compensation within a movement and longer-term adaptation of subsequent movements.

claim: Adaptation is hypothesized to occur whenever a sensory error is perceived, including after a single exposure to altered feedback.
source: Although adaptation is hypothesized to occur whenever a sensory error is perceived (including after a single exposure to altered feedback), adaptation of articulatory movements in speech has only been observed after repeated exposure to auditory perturbations, questioning both current theories of speech sensorimotor adaptation and the universality of more general theories of adaptation.
evidence: This refers to theoretical predictions from sensorimotor adaptation models.

claim: Participants were exposed to intermittent, unpredictable perturbations of their speech acoustics in the study.

claim: Auditory feedback plays a major role in online execution of speech motor plans.
source: Auditory feedback plays a major role in both online execution and refinement of speech motor plans, as observed when the auditory feedback participants receive about their own speech is perturbed in real time (Houde and Jordan, 1998; Purcell and Munhall, 2006b; Tourville et al., 2008; Villacorta et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Consistent perturbations lead to sensorimotor adaptation—a learned change in speech behavior that is observable from the onset of a subsequent speech movement and which persists even after the perturbation is removed.

claim: Compensation and adaptation behaviors are widely considered to be driven by sensory prediction errors.
source: These behaviors are widely considered to be driven by sensory prediction errors (differences between expected and perceived sensory feedback), although models differ in the proposed mechanism by which this occurs.

claim: Sensory prediction errors are differences between expected and perceived sensory feedback.

claim: In the DIVA model, sensory prediction errors lead to feedback-based corrective motor commands.
source: In the DIVA (Directions Into Velocities of Articulators) model (Tourville and Guenther, 2011), sensory prediction errors lead to feedback-based corrective motor commands (i.e., the within-trial compensation response) which are subsequently incorporated into the feedforward motor program used for future productions of the same syllables, creating the adaptation response (Kawato et al., 1987).
evidence: This describes a specific theoretical model with citations.

claim: In the DIVA model, feedback-based corrective motor commands are subsequently incorporated into the feedforward motor program used for future productions of the same syllables, creating the adaptation response.

evidence: This describes a specific theoretical model with citations.

claim: An alternative theoretical account suggests sensory prediction errors directly lead to updates of internal models in the sensorimotor control system.
source: An alternative theoretical account of adaptation (Houde and Nagarajan, 2011) suggests sensory prediction errors instead directly lead to updates of internal models in the sensorimotor control system, either to forward models predicting the sensory outcomes of actions (Bastian, 2006; Haith and Krakauer, 2013; Houde and Nagarajan, 2011; Krakauer and Mazzoni, 2011; Shadmehr et al., 2010), to the control policy guiding action (Hadjiosif et al., 2020), or to both (Wolpert et al., 1998; Wolpert and Kawato, 1998).
evidence: This describes alternative theoretical models with citations.

claim: Both the compensation-based and internal-model hypotheses of sensorimotor adaptation predict that learning in speech occurs progressively.

evidence: This is an inference about what the theories predict.

evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The less reliable within-participant relationship may be more consistent with models of adaptation that rely on updates to internal models compared to models that use feedback corrections to update future feedforward commands.
source: However, the less reliable within-participant relationship may be more consistent with models of adaptation that rely on updates to internal models compared to models that use feedback corrections to update future feedforward commands.
evidence: This is speculation about the theoretical implications of the findings.

claim: Mixed results on the causal relationship between feedback commands and feedforward learning have been reported in the reaching literature.
source: Similarly mixed results on the causal relationship between feedback commands and feedforward learning have been reported in the reaching literature (Albert and Shadmehr, 2016; Kim et al., 2021; Tseng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A single exposure to altered auditory feedback induces 'one-shot' adaptation in the speech sensorimotor system.
source: Overall, these results provide evidence that a single exposure to altered auditory feedback induces 'one-shot' adaptation in the speech sensorimotor system.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings are consistent with current models of adaptation in speech specifically and in human movement more broadly.
source: This is consistent with current models of adaptation in speech specifically and in human movement more broadly; within these frameworks, one-shot adaptation is an effect that may continually build upon itself to create more enduring adaptation responses.
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical implications.

claim: Within current theoretical frameworks, one-shot adaptation is an effect that may continually build upon itself to create more enduring adaptation responses.
source: This is consistent with current models of adaptation in speech specifically and in human movement more broadly; within these frameworks, one-shot adaptation is an effect that may continually build upon itself to create more enduring adaptation responses.
evidence: This is an inference about how one-shot adaptation relates to longer-term adaptation.

claim: Further comparison of single-trial vs. longer-timescale sensorimotor learning in the same individuals is warranted to strengthen the claim about one-shot adaptation building into enduring adaptation.
source: Further comparison of single-trial vs. longer-timescale sensorimotor learning in the same individuals is warranted to strengthen this claim.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: The expected relationship between compensation and adaptation was observed reliably at the participant level and somewhat less reliably at the trial level.
source: The expected relationship between compensation and adaptation was observed reliably at the participant level and somewhat less reliably at the trial level.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: The results provide evidence that adaptation in speech may operate in a similar manner as in other motor domains.
source: Our results provide evidence that adaptation in speech may operate in a similar manner as in other motor domains.
evidence: This is an inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Speech is a well-learned natural behavior that relies primarily on implicit learning.
source: As a well-learned natural behavior that relies primarily on implicit learning, speech offers a unique, ecologically valid paradigm to further our understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving sensorimotor adaptation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about speech as a behavior.

claim: Speech offers a unique, ecologically valid paradigm to further our understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving sensorimotor adaptation.
source: As a well-learned natural behavior that relies primarily on implicit learning, speech offers a unique, ecologically valid paradigm to further our understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving sensorimotor adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference about the value of studying speech for understanding sensorimotor adaptation.

claim: Data were included if participants met inclusion criteria for their respective studies and if the formant shifts they received were opposite or near-opposite each other in 2D formant space (separated by an angle of 180±20° when plotted together in F1/F2 space).
source: Data were included if participants met inclusion criteria for their respective studies and if the formant shifts they received were opposite or near-opposite each other in 2D formant space (separated by an angle of 180±20° when plotted together in F1/F2 space).
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the analysis.

claim: Data from 91 participants met the inclusion criteria.
source: Data from 91 participants met these criteria; 40 of these participants contributed to two of the included studies.
evidence: This describes the sample size.

claim: 40 participants contributed to two of the included studies.
source: Data from 91 participants met these criteria; 40 of these participants contributed to two of the included studies.
evidence: This describes overlap in the sample.

claim: All participants were native speakers of American English.
source: All participants were native speakers of American English and reported no history of speech, hearing, or neurological disorders.
evidence: This describes participant characteristics.

claim: All participants reported no history of speech, hearing, or neurological disorders.
source: All participants were native speakers of American English and reported no history of speech, hearing, or neurological disorders.

claim: Informed consent and consent to publish was obtained for all participants.
source: Informed consent and consent to publish was obtained for all participants.
evidence: This describes ethical procedures.

claim: The experimental protocols were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the institutions from which data were collected.
source: The experimental protocols were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the institutions from which data were collected: the University of Wisconsin–Madison, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of California, San Francisco, and the University of California, Berkeley.
evidence: This describes ethical approval.

claim: In all studies, participants spoke aloud monosyllabic English words containing the vowel /ɛ/.
source: In all studies, participants spoke aloud monosyllabic English words containing the vowel /ɛ/ (as in head), which were presented as text on a screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants heard real-time auditory feedback of their speech through headphones.
source: Simultaneously, participants heard real-time auditory feedback of their speech through headphones.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: On a pseudorandom subset of trials (25–50%), auditory feedback was altered with one of two real-time feedback perturbation systems, Audapter or FUSP.
source: On a pseudorandom subset of trials (25–50%), auditory feedback was altered with one of two real-time feedback perturbation systems, Audapter (Cai et al., 2008; Tourville et al., 2013) or Feedback Utility for Speech Production (FUSP) (Katseff et al., 2012; Parrell et al., 2017; Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with citations.

claim: Linear predictive coding (LPC) was used to model the vowel portion of the signal and apply a formant shift in real time during speech.
source: Briefly, linear predictive coding (LPC) was used to model the vowel portion of the signal and apply a formant shift in real time during speech.
evidence: This describes the technical method used.

claim: Unaltered trials underwent the same processing pipeline but with no alteration to the formants, such that auditory feedback in all trials had the same (minimal) delay.
source: Unaltered trials (50–75% of trials) underwent the same processing pipeline but with no alteration to the formants, such that auditory feedback in all trials had the same (minimal) delay.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The magnitude and direction of the applied formant shift varied slightly across studies.
source: The magnitude and direction of the applied formant shift varied slightly across studies.
evidence: This describes variation in the experimental design.

claim: Studies 1, 2, 3, and 4 shifted F1 upward and downward at a consistent magnitude that was applied to all participants.
source: Studies 1, 2, 3, and 4 shifted F1 upward and downward at a consistent magnitude (in mels or Hz) that was applied to all participants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of specific studies.

claim: For Studies 5 and 6, only the F1 portion of the vector was considered in the analysis.
source: For these studies, only the F1 portion of the vector was considered in the analysis; perturbations that increased F1 (/ɛ/ to /æ/) were considered 'up' shifts and perturbations that decreased F1 (/ɛ/ to /ɪ/) were considered 'down' shifts.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach.

claim: All formant values were converted into mels for purposes of this analysis.
source: All formant values were converted into mels for purposes of this analysis.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach.

claim: Trials with a vowel duration of less than 100 ms were excluded from analysis (<1%).
source: Trials with a vowel duration of less than 100 ms were excluded from analysis (<1%).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Two participants were excluded from the analysis as outliers (average compensation or one-shot response >4 SD from mean).
source: Two participants were excluded from the analysis as outliers (average compensation or one-shot response >4 SD from mean).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Compensation response was operationalized as the mean normalized F1 produced during the 150–250 ms time window of trials in which a perturbation occurred.
source: At the trial level, compensation response was operationalized as the mean normalized F1 produced during the 150–250 ms time window of trials in which a perturbation occurred (perturbation trials).
evidence: This describes the analysis approach.

claim: A 200–300 ms time window was originally planned for the compensation analysis.
source: A 200–300 ms time window was originally planned for this analysis; however, only 46% of produced vowels had a duration of at least 300 ms, whereas 80% of vowels lasted until the end of the 150–250 ms time window.
evidence: This describes a change in the analysis plan.

claim: Only 46% of produced vowels had a duration of at least 300 ms.
source: A 200–300 ms time window was originally planned for this analysis; however, only 46% of produced vowels had a duration of at least 300 ms, whereas 80% of vowels lasted until the end of the 150–250 ms time window.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data.

claim: 80% of vowels lasted until the end of the 150–250 ms time window.
source: A 200–300 ms time window was originally planned for this analysis; however, only 46% of produced vowels had a duration of at least 300 ms, whereas 80% of vowels lasted until the end of the 150–250 ms time window.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data.

claim: One-shot adaptation response was calculated as the mean normalized F1 produced in the first 100 ms of unperturbed trials that occurred directly after a perturbed trial.
source: At the trial level, one-shot adaptation response was calculated as the mean normalized F1 produced in the first 100 ms of unperturbed trials that occurred directly after a perturbed trial (post-perturbation trials).
evidence: This describes the analysis approach.

claim: Only F1 values from the initial 100 ms of the vowel were included in the one-shot adaptation analysis, limiting the influence of auditory-based feedback control mechanisms, which have a latency of 100–150 ms in speech.
source: Only F1 values from the initial 100 ms of the vowel were included, limiting the influence of auditory-based feedback control mechanisms, which have a latency of 100–150 ms in speech (Cai et al., 2012; Parrell et al., 2017; Tourville et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the analysis approach, supported by citations.

claim: Auditory-based feedback control mechanisms have a latency of 100–150 ms in speech.
source: Only F1 values from the initial 100 ms of the vowel were included, limiting the influence of auditory-based feedback control mechanisms, which have a latency of 100–150 ms in speech (Cai et al., 2012; Parrell et al., 2017; Tourville et al., 2008).
